title: How Much Does Fraud Detection Cost for a Nigerian Fintech?
summary: Fraud detection pricing is rarely published. See how it is priced, what drives the cost for a Nigerian fintech, and the questions to ask before you sign.
body_markdown:
You lead a product or risk team at a Nigerian fintech and need a fraud detection partner. That means putting a number in the budget, so the search starts with cost. Across different providers, almost every pricing page gives the same answer: "contact sales." The next step is a call, and a week later you have various options without knowing which is the better fit.


This matters more now. Under the CBN's


[Baseline Standards for Automated AML Solutions](https://www.cbn.gov.ng/Out/2026/CCD/CBN%20issues%20Baseline%20Standards%20for%20Automated%20Anti-Money%20Laundering%20Solution.pdf) , every regulated institution, including payment service providers, must run automated transaction monitoring. Fraud controls are expected to work in real time or near real time, so the question is no longer whether to budget, but how much.


This guide explains how fraud detection is priced, what pushes the cost up or down, and what to ask before you sign, so you can compare quotes on fit and not just price.


### **Why Fraud Detection Pricing Is Hard to Compare Across Vendors**


Fraud detection software pricing in Nigeria rarely comes with a price list, because four things change the number:


- **Volume:** A fintech monitoring 5,000 transactions a month is priced differently from one monitoring five million.


- **What you screen:** Monitoring transfers is different from screening sign-ups, loan applications or payments, and each event type can be priced differently.


- **How you integrate:** A ready-made rule template and a clean API tend to cost less to set up than a custom build with a dedicated team.


- **What "fraud detection" bundles:** Rules, machine learning scoring, case management and reporting. Vendors package these differently, so two quotes rarely compare like for like.


That is why *"contact sales"* is the usual answer. A vendor cannot quote until it knows your volume, your event types and what you want included. Once you know what drives the price, the pricing models make more sense.


### **Common Pricing Models**


Most vendors use one of four models, or a blend of them. For each, here is how it works, who it suits and what to watch for.


**Per event:** You pay for each transaction or check the system processes, so the bill follows your traffic. A month with twice the transactions costs roughly twice as much, and a quiet month costs less. It suits low or unpredictable volume, because you only pay for what you use. Watch for costs that climb quickly in busy months, and for a rate that does not come down as your volume grows.


**Per decision:** You pay for each decision the system makes, such as approve, reject or refer. The meter runs on verdicts, not on raw traffic. It suits teams that want cost tied to outcomes. Watch what counts as a billable decision, because a referral to manual review may be billed differently from an approval, and ask whether a retried event counts as a second decision.


**Subscription:** You pay a fixed fee tied to expected monthly volume, so you know the number before the month starts. Plans are usually built in tiers, and you pick the one that fits your volume. It suits steady volume and easier budgeting. Watch for overage charges when you go past your tier, and check whether you can move up a tier mid-contract if you grow faster than planned.


**Prepaid credits:** You top up a balance and each event draws it down, so spend is capped by what you load. When the balance runs out, processing stops until you top up, so low-balance alerts matter. It suits teams that want tight control. Watch for expiry dates and minimum top-ups.


When you compare quotes, convert each one to a monthly cost at your own volume. Many vendors also blend these models, for example a subscription for the core service plus per-event charges above a set limit. The model matters, but what really moves the bill is what happens around it.


### **What Pushes the Cost Up**


Five things inflate the bill beyond the price on the quote:


- **Volume spikes:** Busy periods, such as the December rush, can push you into a higher tier or trigger overage charges.


- **False positives:** Every wrongly flagged event costs review time and can annoy a genuine customer.


- **Analyst time:** The people reviewing alerts are often the biggest cost, and it grows with alert volume.


- **Disconnected tools:** Separate tools for verification, monitoring and review mean duplicate integration work, duplicate data and alerts nobody connects.


- **Heavy checks on low-risk events:** Applying expensive checks to every event raises spend without adding protection.


Onboarding checks have their own costs, which our guide to


[KYC pricing in Nigeria](https://dojah.io/blog/kyc-pricing-nigeria) covers. The good news is that most of what is listed here can be controlled.


### **What Brings It Down**


Cutting cost should not mean cutting protection. NIBSS reported that


[industry fraud losses in Nigeria were ₦25.85 billion in 2025](https://allafrica.com/stories/202601230595.html) , so a cheaper tool that misses fraud is not a saving. The aim is to spend where the risk is:


- **Match checks to risk:** Apply stronger checks to higher-risk events, such as a first transfer to a new beneficiary, and keep low-risk events light.


- **Fewer false alerts:** Tune rules over time, and test each change on past events before it goes live, so a new rule does not flood your queue.


- **One connected stack:** When verification, monitoring and case review share data, fewer cases need a second look. The CBN expects the same: its Standards say an AML solution without effective links to customer KYC data will not be regarded as compliant.


- **Start small:** Begin with one flow or one decision type, such as bank transfers, and expand once you see the results.


- **Negotiate volume early:** Raise it before costs are already growing, while you still have room to shape the terms.


Before you commit, ask the right questions.


### **Questions to Ask Any Vendor**


Take these seven to every vendor, and ask for the answers in writing:


1. **What exactly is billable: an event, a decision, an alert or a case?** If the vendor can't name one clear unit, the bill will surprise you.


2. **Are flagged and blocked events billed the same as allowed ones?** You may pay for every event, including the ones that turn out to be nothing.


3. **What alert rate should I expect at my volume, and who tunes the rules to bring it down?** More alerts mean more analyst hours, which is often your biggest cost.


4. **What happens at peak volume, and what are the overage rates?** Ask what a December rush would cost.


5. **Are there minimums, seat fees or contract lengths, and what changes at renewal?** A low rate can come with a high floor, and the rate, tier or terms may move after year one.


6. **Is testing, sandbox use or loading historical data billed?** You will test rules and backfill past events before going live, so find out whether that costs extra.


7. **Are case management and reporting included or extra?** That is where your analysts spend their time.


Compare the answers, not just the headline rate. A low price per event can hide charges that a higher, simpler price does not.

To estimate your cost:


1. Count your monthly events, split by type: transfers, payments, sign-ups.


2. Estimate the share that needs human review.


3. Ask for a quote at that volume, and at double it, so you can see how the price moves as you grow.
